preamble: Deaspiration of [pʰ] to plain [p]. The documented case is Grassmann's law in Ancient Greek, a dissimilation whereby the first of two aspirates in successive syllables loses aspiration; it shows up in reduplicated perfects of φ-initial roots and in inherited words such as παχύς 'thick' (PIE *bʰénǵʰus, with *bʰ > pʰ and then deaspiration before the following χ). Sanskrit applies the same deaspiration in reduplication (Whitney §590a).

examples.to: πέφυκα péphūka 'I have grown, I am by nature'
examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses aspiration before the aspirated root-initial φ.
Root-internal Grassmann's law: *bʰ became pʰ in Greek and then lost its aspiration before the aspirate χ of the next syllable; cognate Sanskrit bahú 'much'.

sources: Whitney, W. D. (1889). Sanskrit Grammar, §590a (deaspiration in reduplication). https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Sanskrit_Grammar_by_Whitney_p1.djvu/250
